hook_patterns: Hypothesis: Open with [REPORTED TRANSACTION AMOUNT], then ask what it means relative to [RELEVANT COMPARISON] rather than treating it as a buy signal.
Hypothesis: Put [PRICE CHANGE] beside [BUSINESS METRIC], then identify the question needed to reconcile them.
Hypothesis: Present the decision as [OPTION A] versus [OPTION B], with [MEASURABLE CONDITION] as the dividing line.
Hypothesis: Demonstrate one [PUBLIC-DATA LOOKUP], then explain one limitation before interpreting the result.
Hypothesis: Explain [FINANCING MECHANISM] through an everyday budget analogy, with an original dry aside such as 'The spreadsheet does not accept enthusiasm as collateral.'
packaging_notes: Insider tracking is a transferable lead: the tool explainer records 239.5x its baseline across 7 prior uploads; a company-specific insider-purchase video records 5.2x across 17. Both are strong-tier signals. Transaction amounts in titles remain unverified claims, not established financial facts.

Company-specific decisions and industry updates recur among strong-tier candidates: NVIDIA decision framing reaches 19.5x, a four-stock post-selloff list reaches 5.7x, and semiconductor updates reach 4.4–4.5x. These associations do not establish which packaging element drove views.

Use numbers to define the subject: transaction amounts, time windows and a bounded stock count. Metadata does not show that greater numerical precision improves performance. Avoid turning purchases, analyst opinions or price moves into automatic investment recommendations.

There is no demonstrated duration sweet spot. Strong-tier examples span 36 seconds to 35 minutes 50 seconds; the two strongest baseline multiples run 87 and 36 seconds. The <=180-second bucket does not establish Shorts status, and long-video runtimes should not guide Shorts length.

AI-debt explanation at 13.8x and an event-outcome question at 2.9x are emerging-tier evidence only. Treat all patterns as test candidates, not proven weekly winners: the supplied uploads span September 28–October 23, baselines are not equal-age, and no opening-line or retention data is available. Exclude crash urgency and sweeping buy-signal claims.
market_patterns.title: outlier pattern extraction

winning_patterns: Among the three Shorts, a company-led headline pairing an extreme percentage move with a corporate-action explanation had the strongest retention: 90.6% average viewed and 1.242 hook hold. This supports testing anomaly-plus-explanation framing, not assuming extreme numbers drive reach.

A ticker-led Short pairing a price-target revision with a specific dollar level and named analyst firm retained 74.0% on average, with 1.053 hook hold. A concrete valuation change is a promising structure to retest.
losing_patterns: The only long video combined an executive role, transaction amount, timing and filing terminology. Its 37.1% average viewed and 0.644 hook hold make this information-dense setup worth simplifying in a test, but one long video cannot establish that the title structure caused weaker retention.

Within Shorts, the large positive percentage-move headline had the weakest retention: 66.8% average viewed and 1.074 hook hold. Avoid treating a dramatic gain figure or the highest view count as evidence of the strongest viewer hold; this is not evidence that gain-led titles generally underperform.
notes: Only four videos, with 89–239 views each, are supplied. These are tentative correlations; actual opening scripts are unavailable, so hook-framing conclusions are limited to headline promises and hook-hold measurements.
The two market_close Shorts span the highest and lowest Short retention, so there is no consistent franchise winner. analyst_shock and insider_watch each have only one observation.

Analyze the single long video separately from the three Shorts. Average viewed is not swipe-away or feed conversion; hook-hold values above 1.0 do not establish broad audience demand or title-driven distribution.
